question: Which `mistral-vespa` commands do I run to create a migration and deploy it?
reference_answer:
`mistral-vespa generate-migration --app-dir <dir> <name>` scaffolds the migration you fill in.
`mistral-vespa migrate --app-dir <dir> --config-server <url> --query-port <port>` builds the application package and deploys it.
answer_text:
**Create migration:**

```bash
uv run mistral-vespa generate-migration --app-dir ./vespa_app <name>
```
Example: `uv run mistral-vespa generate-migration --app-dir ./vespa_app initial_schema`

Creates timestamped file under `vespa_app/migrations/` with a `VespaMigration` stub.

**Deploy it:**

```bash
uv run mistral-vespa migrate \
  --app-dir ./vespa_app \
  --config-server http://localhost:19171 \
  --query-port 18080
```
`migrate` discovers migrations, runs them in order, builds the app package in-memory, uploads it, and polls query endpoint until up.

> `uv run mistral-vespa generate --app-dir ./vespa_app --path ./vespa.lock` only writes package to disk for inspection/CI — **not used for deployment.**

Documentation used:

* [Manage schema – Create and evolve schemas](https://docs.mistral.ai/studio/search/search-toolkit/vespa/migrations)
* [Local development – Step 1: Create migration / Step 3: Deploy](https://docs.mistral.ai/studio/search/search-toolkit/vespa/local-development)
* [CLI reference – `generate-migration` / `migrate` / `generate`](https://docs.mistral.ai/studio/search/search-toolkit/search-index/vespa/cli)

question: What file formats and what maximum size can I upload for OCR? A .zip upload comes back as 422 `Invalid file format.`
reference_answer:
OCR accepts PDF, Office documents (DOCX, PPTX, XLSX/CSV), text formats such as TXT, EPUB, RTF, ODT and LaTeX, and images (JPEG, PNG, AVIF, TIFF, GIF, HEIC, BMP, WebP); ZIP is not among them.
Uploads are capped at 512 MB, OCR documents at 50 MB and 1,000 pages, and files are kept 30 days.
answer_text:
For `POST /v1/files` + `POST /v1/ocr`:

**Maximum size: `512 MB` per file.**

> `The size of individual files can be a maximum of 512 MB.`
> https://docs.mistral.ai/api/endpoint/files

> `Maximum file size: 512 MB`
> https://docs.mistral.ai/resources/known-limitations

**Supported formats for OCR:**

> `Supported formats for OCR: PDF, PNG, JPG, JPEG, TIFF, BMP, GIF, WEBP`
> https://docs.mistral.ai/resources/known-limitations

The OCR processor docs distinguish:

* `image_url`: `PNG, JPEG/JPG, AVIF, and other image formats`
* `document_url`: `PDF, PPTX, DOCX, and other document formats`
* https://docs.mistral.ai/studio/document-processing/basic_ocr

**Why `.zip` -> `422 Invalid file format`:**

`.zip` is in neither list. It is not an OCR-supported image/document format, so the Files / OCR validation rejects it with `422`.

Fix: extract the archive locally and upload the contained `PDF / PNG / JPG / JPEG / TIFF / BMP / GIF / WEBP` files individually (each ≤512MB), then call OCR per file.

question: How do I select a page range for an OCR request, and where does page numbering start?

question: Does the Postgres backend scope queries from the retrieval context the way Vespa does?
reference_answer:
No: Postgres accepts the ingest and retrieval contexts but only propagates them, applying no `group_id` or `yql_filter` scoping, so every query sees the whole collection.
Isolate each tenant in its own collection and table, or filter before the store.
answer_text:
No.

In Mistral's Search Toolkit, `PostgresStoreIndex` uses the same `VectorStoreIndex` / `Pipeline` / `QueryEngine` interfaces as Vespa, but **query scoping differs**:

> `IngestContext` and `RetrievalContext` are accepted by every entry point, but the backend only propagates them. **The Postgres backend doesn't derive query scope from these contexts.** Unlike the Vespa backend, it doesn't apply `group_id` or `yql_filter` for tenant isolation. Every query can see the full collection. [Postgres - No context-derived filtering](https://docs.mistral.ai/studio/search/search-toolkit/search-index/postgres#no-context-derived-filtering)

Consequences stated in docs:

* Warning: `The Postgres backend doesn't derive tenant filters from IngestContext or RetrievalContext.` [Postgres](https://docs.mistral.ai/studio/search/search-toolkit/search-index/postgres)
* Mitigation: `Isolate each tenant in a separate collection and table, or apply filtering before the store.` Same page.
* Overview: `Both built-in backends implement the VectorStoreIndex protocol, so they use the same ingestion and retrieval pipeline interfaces. Their provisioning, schema management, and query-scoping behavior differ.` [Search index](https://docs.mistral.ai/studio/search/search-toolkit/search-index)

question: Can an agent combine the built-in web search tool with a JSON response format?
reference_answer:
The documentation does not say whether a structured response format may be combined with the built-in web search tool.
It documents each separately and never states the combination's behaviour.
answer_text:
Yes.

An Agent using `web_search` / `web_search_premium` **can** set a JSON `response_format`:

* Agents Introduction lists as supported in Agents / Conversations API: `Built-in connector tools for ... web search ...` plus `Features supported via our chat completions endpoint are also supported, such as: Structured Outputs`: https://docs.mistral.ai/capabilities/agents

* Custom structured output definition with `response_format` schema: https://docs.mistral.ai/studio/conversations/structured-output/custom

1. question: A one-page 308 kB PDF sent as base64 to Document QnA reports 321,774 prompt tokens and 400s — what is the context limit and why is the document so expensive?
reference_answer:
Document QnA has its own document and page limits, and the request still has to fit the model's context window — 256k tokens on Medium 3.5, Small 4 and Large 3, 128k on Medium 3.1.
Requests over the window come back as 400, and token counts cover input plus output.
answer_text:
Your `400`:

> `Prompt contains 321774 tokens ... too large for model with 262144 maximum context length`

is the **model context-window check**.

### 1. Context limit

`262,144` tokens is that model's limit.

Documented limits per model:

* `Mistral Large 3 / Medium 3.5 / Small 4 / Ministral 3 / Devstral 2: 256k`
* `Medium 3.1 / Codestral / Magistral Medium 1.2 / Nemo 12B: 128k`
* Requests exceeding the window return `400 Bad Request`. `prompt_tokens + max_tokens` must fit.

Pages used:

* Document QnA: https://docs.mistral.ai/studio-api/document-processing/document_qna
* Known limitations - Context window / File uploads / Vision: https://docs.mistral.ai/resources/known-limitations

Full up to date list: model cards linked from that page.

### 2. Why 1 page / 308 kB = 321,774 prompt tokens

That is not the extracted text. A 455-word page would be ~1-2k tokens after OCR.

What happened is the **raw base64 string was counted as prompt tokens**.

`308 kB PDF -> ~410k base64 chars -> ~321k tokens`, and it also explains:

* `128 kB` PDF succeeding but reporting `~1.3M`? / huge `prompt_tokens` unrelated to word count.
* `400s` latency: model has to ingest a 321k-token prompt.

This exact pattern was reported as Mistral bug:

> `[BUG CLIENT]: Base64 url counting towards token limit when using Document QnA` - 1-page 308 kB PDF -> `321774 tokens ... 262144 maximum`
> https://github.com/mistralai/client-python/issues/502

Mistral closed it as `fixed on our end`.

### Fix

Do not send `data:application/pdf;base64,...` in `document_url` / chat `content` for Document QnA. Use the documented path:

1. `document_url` with **public URL**: https://docs.mistral.ai/studio-api/document-processing/document_qna
2. Uploaded file, or
3. `client.ocr.process(model="mistral-ocr-latest", ...)` first, then send only extracted markdown/text to `chat.complete`: https://docs.mistral.ai/studio/document-processing/basic_ocr

That reduces this case from `321,774` to `~1-2k` prompt tokens.

question: The docs show `client.files.upload(..., purpose="ocr")` but my type checker says only `fine-tune` and `batch` are valid — which values does the file upload endpoint actually accept?
reference_answer:

> `purpose # "fine-tune"|"batch"|"ocr"`

> curl https://api.mistral.ai/v1/files \

>   -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_APIKEY_HERE" \
>   -F "file=@example.file" \
>   -F "purpose=ocr" \
>   -F "visibility=workspace"

question: Can I point the Vespa client at different hosts for querying and for feeding documents?
reference_answer:
The client configuration is documented with a single `endpoint` plus timeout, retry and TLS settings.
Nothing describes separate query and feed endpoints.
answer_text:
Yes.

Use `VespaClientConfig` with separate `query_endpoint` and `feed_endpoint`, instead of single `endpoint`:

```python
from mistralai.search.toolkit.plugins.vespa import VespaClientConfig
from vespa_app import app

client_config = VespaClientConfig(
    query_endpoint="https://query.vespa.example.com",
    feed_endpoint="https://feed.vespa.example.com",
)
vector_store = app.get_search_index(
    client_config=client_config,
    collection_name="articles",
)
```

* Single `endpoint` is documented as:

> `Use app.get_search_index() for the common case where a single endpoint serves both query and feed APIs`

* Separate endpoints are documented as:

> `Use separate query and feed endpoints for production deployments`

Sources:

* Configuration docs: https://pypi.org/project/mistralai-search-toolkit-plugins-vespa/
* Background - Vespa supports different query/feed endpoints when `<search/>` and `<document-api/>` are in separate container clusters: https://docs.vespa.ai/en/operations/self-managed/container.html

question: Can Document QnA answer questions about an image (.png, .jpg), or does it only take PDFs?
reference_answer:
The Document QnA pages only ever show PDFs, passed by URL or as a base64 document.
Nothing states whether an uploaded image can be used as the document of a QnA request.
answer_text:
On Mistral's platform, `Document QnA` as documented is **PDF-centric**, but **not PDF-only** for document understanding in general:

* [Document AI QnA](https://docs.mistral.ai/studio/document-processing/document_qna) page:
  > "The examples below show how to interact with a **PDF document** using natural language."
  
  All 3 examples are:
  `QnA with a PDF Url / QnA with a Base64 Encoded PDF / QnA with an Uploaded PDF` using:
  ```json
  {"type": "document_url", "document_url": "https://arxiv.org/pdf/..."}
  ```

* Underlying OCR it uses **does** take images:
  [OCR Processor](https://docs.mistral.ai/studio/document-processing/basic_ocr):
  > "`image_url`: PNG, JPEG/JPG, AVIF, and other image formats."
  > "`document_url`: PDF, PPTX, DOCX, and other document formats."

  With `image_url` example:
  ```python
  client.ocr.process(
    model="mistral-ocr-latest",
    document={"type": "image_url", "image_url": ".../receipt.png"}
  )
  ```

* [Chat with your Documents with built-in Document QnA Cookbook](https://docs.mistral.ai/resources/cookbooks/mistral-ocr-document_understanding):
  > "In this guide, we will demonstrate how to use OCR with our models to discuss **any text-based document, whether it's a PDF, photo, or screenshot**, via URLs and our built-in feature."

**Practical answer for `.png` / `.jpg`:**

1. Don't send it as `type: document_url` - that chunk type is for PDFs in the QnA docs.
2. Do either:
   a. `client.ocr.process(... {"type":"image_url",...})` then pass markdown to chat, or
   b. Chat vision directly with `type: image_url` - see [Vision](https://docs.mistral.ai/studio-api/conversations/vision): "There are two ways to send an image to the Chat Completions API, either by passing a URL or by passing a base64 encoded image."

question: Which models support custom structured outputs? `chat.parse` with a pydantic response format raises a JSON decode error on the model I picked.
reference_answer:
The custom structured output page lists the models that support it; a model outside that list may return text that is not valid JSON.
JSON mode is the weaker fallback and guarantees valid JSON but not schema adherence.
answer_text:
On Mistral La Plateforme:

### Which models support Custom Structured Outputs (`response_format` = Pydantic / `json_schema`)?

**All currently available models except `codestral-mamba`.**

> Docs FAQ: “All currently available models except for `codestral-mamba` are supported.”

* Source: [Custom Structured Outputs – FAQ: Which models support custom Structured Outputs?](https://docs.mistral.ai/studio/conversations/structured-output/custom)
* Same rule for JSON Mode (`{"type":"json_object"}`): [JSON Mode – FAQ: Which models support JSON Mode?](https://docs.mistral.ai/studio/conversations/structured-output/json_mode) – “All currently available models except for …”
* Overview: [Structured Outputs](https://docs.mistral.ai/studio/conversations/structured-output)
* API reference: [Chat Endpoints – `response_format`: `json_object` / `json_schema`](https://docs.mistral.ai/api/endpoint/chat)

### Why does `chat.parse(..., response_format=MyPydanticModel)` raise `JSON decode error`?

That is the expected failure when the selected model does not enforce the schema – most commonly:

1. You picked an unsupported model – e.g. `codestral-mamba`, an embedding (`mistral-embed`), moderation, OCR, or audio/transcription model. Switch to e.g. `mistral-large-latest`, `mistral-small-latest`, `ministral-8b-latest`.
2. You used `chat.complete()` instead of `chat.parse()`. Only `parse` validates/parses against the Pydantic / Zod / JSON Schema. Example from docs:
```python
from mistralai import Mistral
client = Mistral(api_key=api_key)
chat_response = client.chat.parse(
  model="ministral-8b-latest",
  messages=[...],
  response_format=Book, # Pydantic BaseModel
)
```
See [Custom Structured Outputs – Usage](https://docs.mistral.ai/studio/conversations/structured-output/custom).

3. If supplying raw JSON Schema via `chat.complete()`, it must be strict: include `"additionalProperties": False` and `"strict": True`. See [mistralai/client-python `structured_outputs_with_json_schema.py`](https://github.com/mistralai/client-python/blob/main/examples/mistral/chat/structured_outputs_with_json_schema.py).

Check `chat_response.choices[0].message.content` (raw JSON string) vs. parsed output to isolate whether the model returned non-JSON.

question: Which models can take a document as input in a chat message, and how do I pass it?
reference_answer:
Document QnA is the documented path: send a `document_url` content chunk alongside your `text` chunk, with a publicly reachable URL or a base64 data URI.
The worked examples run it on `mistral-small-latest`.
answer_text:

question: How do I count the tokens of a prompt locally, before sending the request?
reference_answer:
The documentation does not describe a local tokenizer or a token-counting endpoint.
It reports token usage only in the response of a call that has already been made.
answer_text:
To count tokens locally use Mistral's open-source `mistral-common` tokenizer - no API call:

```python
pip install mistral-common
```

```python
from mistral_common.protocol.instruct.messages import UserMessage
from mistral_common.protocol.instruct.request import ChatCompletionRequest
from mistral_common.tokens.tokenizers.mistral import MistralTokenizer

tokenizer = MistralTokenizer.v3(is_tekken=True)
model_name = "nemostral"

tokenized = tokenizer.encode_chat_completion(
  ChatCompletionRequest(
    messages=[UserMessage(content="What's the weather like today in Paris")],
    model=model_name,
  )
)
tokens, text = tokenized.tokens, tokenized.text
print(len(tokens)) # number of tokens, e.g. `128`
```

> Use `encode_chat_completion()` for a full prompt with messages/tools, then `len(tokens)`.

This is required because billing / context limits count `prompt + max_tokens`, including control tokens (`[INST]`, etc.) and tool descriptions added by the chat template - simple word/character counting is not accurate.

question: What does the API return when the model name in a request does not exist, and what shape does the error body have?
reference_answer:
Every error is a JSON body with `object`, `message`, `type`, `param` and `code`; for an unknown model, `param` is `model` and `code` is `unknown_model`.

* **Body shape:** all API errors return JSON with this structure: https://docs.mistral.ai/resources/error-glossary

```json
{
  "object": "error",
  "message": "A human-readable description of the error.",
  "type": "invalid_request_error",
  "param": "model",
  "code": "unknown_model"
}
```

Fields documented on that page:

> `type` - Error category (`invalid_request_error`, `authentication_error`, `rate_limit_error`, `server_error`)
> `param` - The parameter that caused the error (if applicable)
> `code` - Machine-readable error code (if applicable)

question: What changed in Search Toolkit 0.0.13, and does the old schema call still work?
reference_answer:
The 0.0.13 entry lists the breaking changes, including the schema's move to `embedding_model`.
The deprecated form still runs with a warning, but passing both spellings raises.
answer_text:
In `0.0.13` the **schema embedding config** is breaking:

**Changed:** `create_schema()` / `create_default_schema()` now take `embedding_model: EmbeddingModel | MistralEmbeddingPreset` instead of `embedding_dimensions: int`:

> `create_schema()` and `create_default_schema()` now take `embedding_model` ... instead of `embedding_dimensions: int`.

* `VespaSchemaDefinition.embedding_dimensions` -> `embedding_model: EmbeddingModel`, threading `name, dimensions, dtype, distance metric` through. `VespaSearchIndex` now exposes `embedding_model`.
* New abstraction: `MistralEmbeddingModel` / `CustomEmbeddingModel`, `MistralEmbeddingPreset.MISTRAL_EMBED_DIM_1024/_256/_128` + `build_embedding_model()`, `VectorDType`, `DistanceMetric`.

New canonical call:

```python
create_schema(
 name="articles",
 mode=SearchMode.INDEX,
 embedding_model=MistralEmbeddingPreset.MISTRAL_EMBED_DIM_1024,
 indexing_mode=IndexingMode.DOCUMENT_PER_CHUNK,
 fields=[...]
)
```

**Does old call still work? Yes, temporarily:**

> `embedding_dimensions` is deprecated (emits a `DeprecationWarning` and builds a `CustomEmbeddingModel(name="unknown")` under the hood); passing both raises `ValueError`.

> `create_default_schema(...)` is deprecated. It only produces the legacy `IndexingMode.SINGLE_DOCUMENT` field set and will be removed before `1.0.0`. Use `create_schema(..., indexing_mode=...)` instead.

Migrate to `create_schema(..., embedding_model=..., indexing_mode=IndexingMode.DOCUMENT_PER_CHUNK)`.

question: What do `tool_choice` and `parallel_tool_calls` do on a chat completion request, and which values does `tool_choice` take?
reference_answer:
`tool_choice` is `none` (never call a tool), `auto` (model decides), `any`/`required` (must call one or more), or `{"type": "function", "function": {"name": ...}}` to force one tool.
`parallel_tool_calls` enables the model to call several tools in one turn.
answer_text:
On Mistral's `POST /v1/chat/completions`:

* **`tool_choice` :** Controls which (if any) tool is called by the model.
* **`parallel_tool_calls: boolean` , default `true`:** Whether to enable parallel function calling during tool use, when enabled the model can call multiple tools in parallel.

Values for `tool_choice`:

* `"none"` : model will not call any tool and instead generates a message.
* `"auto"` : model can pick between generating a message or calling one or more tools.
* `"any"` or `"required"` : model must call one or more tools.
* Specific tool: `{"type": "function", "function": {"name": "my_function"}}` forces the model to call that tool.

Sources:

* Chat Completion API reference – `tool_choice` and `parallel_tool_calls` definitions: https://docs.mistral.ai/api/endpoint/chat

question: What must a migration define before `mistral-vespa migrate` will deploy it?
reference_answer:
A migration subclasses `VespaMigration` and its `migrate()` must set the application name and create at least one schema.
The deploy step then builds the application package from the whole migration chain.
answer_text:
A `VespaMigration` subclass with `migrate()` that sets app-name + schema:

1. **Location / form:** Python file under `vespa_app/migrations/`, append-only, ordered by timestamp, re-run on every deploy. Stub from `mistral-vespa generate-migration`:

```python
from mistralai.search.toolkit.plugins.vespa.migration import VespaMigration
class MyMigration(VespaMigration):
    def migrate(self) -> None:
        pass # Define your changes here
```
[Manage schema](https://docs.mistral.ai/studio/search/search-toolkit/search-index/vespa/migrations)

2. **Required in first migration:** `set_app_name(app_name: str)` — lowercase `a-z` only:
> `Set the application name for the migration run. Required in the first migration. Must contain only lowercase letters (a-z).`
[Migration helpers reference – `set_app_name`](https://docs.mistral.ai/studio/search/search-toolkit/search-index/vespa/migration-helpers)

3. **Required schema definition:** `create_schema(...)` with required:

   * `name: str` – lowercase + underscores only
   * `mode: SearchMode` – `INDEX` or `STREAMING`
   * `indexing_mode: IndexingMode` – `DOCUMENT_PER_CHUNK` recommended, `SINGLE_DOCUMENT` legacy/deprecated
   * `embedding_model` – e.g. `MistralEmbeddingPreset.MISTRAL_EMBED_DIM_1024`, required unless deprecated `embedding_dimensions`

Example deployable migration:

```python
class InitialSchema(VespaMigration):
    def migrate(self) -> None:
        set_app_name("myapp")
        create_schema(
            name="articles",
            mode=SearchMode.INDEX,
            embedding_model=MistralEmbeddingPreset.MISTRAL_EMBED_DIM_1024,
            indexing_mode=IndexingMode.DOCUMENT_PER_CHUNK,
        )
```
[Migration helpers reference – `VespaMigration` / `create_schema`](https://docs.mistral.ai/studio/search/search-toolkit/search-index/vespa/migration-helpers)

`mistral-vespa migrate` then `discovers migrations, runs them in order, builds the app package, and uploads it.`

question: Pipe characters inside table cells break the Markdown tables OCR returns — is there an output format that does not use pipes as delimiters?
reference_answer:
Yes: `table_format="html"` returns each table as HTML, where cell content is delimited by tags rather than pipes.
`table_format="markdown"` still separates the tables out but keeps the pipe delimiters.
answer_text:
Yes. Use `table_format="html"` — HTML uses `<table>/<tr>/<td>` tags, not `|` delimiters, so cell content containing `|` cannot create extra columns.

From Mistral docs:

> **Table formatting** supports `null`, `markdown`, and `html` values through the `table_format` parameter.
> - `null`: Returns tables inline as Markdown within the extracted page.
> - `markdown`: Returns tables separately as Markdown tables.
> - `html`: Returns tables separately as HTML tables.

> When OCR extracts images and tables, the Markdown output uses placeholders such as `[tbl-3.html](tbl-3.html)` — Use the `images` and `tables` fields to map each placeholder to the extracted image or table.

Example:

```python
ocr_response = client.ocr.process(
    model="mistral-ocr-latest",
    document={
        "type": "document_url",
        "document_url": "https://arxiv.org/pdf/2201.04234"
    },
    table_format="html",
)
```

Then parse `pages[i].tables[]` (`format: "html"`) instead of parsing Markdown tables.

question: What are the stages of an ingestion `Pipeline`, and which of them are required? Mine raises a TypeError about a missing argument.
reference_answer:
A pipeline chains loader, extractor, text splitter, embedder and stores; the extractor is a stage in its own right and cannot be left out.
For PDFs the extractor becomes `MistralOCRExtractor` instead of `PlainTextExtractor`.
answer_text:
An ingestion `Pipeline` chains **5 required + 1 optional** stages:

**Required:**

1. `loader: FileLoader` - reads raw bytes -> `File`
2. `extractor: DocumentExtractor` - `File` -> structured `Document`
3. `text_splitter: TextSplitter` - `Document` -> `DocumentChunk[]`
4. `embedder: Embedder` - chunk -> vector
5. `stores: vector_store / SearchIndex` - persists vector + text

**Optional:**

6. `processors` / `chunk_enrichers: DocumentProcessor[]` e.g. `SummaryEnricher`, `EntityTagger` - adds metadata before indexing. Also optional `checkpoint_store`, `mime_registry`, `protocol_overrides` for `RoutedPipeline`.

> `TypeError: missing argument` means you omitted one of 1-5. Add it to `Pipeline(...)`.

Example - all required present, `processors` optional:

```python
pipeline = Pipeline(
 loader=FilesystemFileLoader(),
 extractor=PlainTextExtractor(),
 text_splitter=CharacterTextSplitter(chunk_size=512),
 processors=[SummaryEnricher(llm_provider=llm)], # optional
 embedder=MistralEmbedder(client=mistral_client, model_name=MODEL_1024_EMBEDDING),
 stores=vector_store,
)
```

https://docs.mistral.ai/studio/search/search-toolkit/ingestion

question: Which models take `reasoning_effort`, and what does each value do?
reference_answer:
`mistral-small-latest` and `mistral-medium-3-5` accept `reasoning_effort` on any chat completion, with `high` recommended for agentic and code work.
`high` returns a full thinking chunk before the answer; `none` makes the model think minimally and omits the chunk.
answer_text:
Per Mistral docs:

### Which models take `reasoning_effort`

Only adjustable-reasoning models:

* `mistral-small-latest`
* `mistral-medium-3-5` — `reasoning_effort="high"` recommended for agentic / code use cases

Source: [Reasoning – Before you start](https://docs.mistral.ai/studio/conversations/reasoning)

> `reasoning_effort` is also available on Agents and Conversations endpoints via `completion_args`.

Deprecated native-reasoning models `magistral-small-latest` / `magistral-medium-latest` **do not** take `reasoning_effort` — reasoning is always-on. See: [Native reasoning (deprecated)](https://docs.mistral.ai/resources/deprecated/native-reasoning)

### What each value does

The Reasoning guide documents only two values:

* `"high"`: includes full thinking chunk (`ThinkChunk` + `TextChunk`) before final answer, at cost of increased token usage. `message.content` becomes `list[ThinkChunk, TextChunk]`.
* `"none"`: thinks minimally, thinking chunk omitted. `message.content` is plain `str`.

Source: [Reasoning – Model / Handling thinking chunks](https://docs.mistral.ai/studio/conversations/reasoning)

The [Chat Completion API Reference](https://docs.mistral.ai/api/endpoint/chat) lists the schema as:

`"none" | "minimal" | "low" | "medium" | "high" | "xhigh"`

but provides **no per-value definition** for `minimal / low / medium / xhigh`. Only `high` / `none` behavior is currently documented.

question: When is `RRFRanker` the right way to do hybrid search, and what does it need in front of it?
reference_answer:
RRF fusion is for the case where you have separate vector and custom keyword stores: run both retrievers and pass `RRFRanker` as a reranker on the query engine.
With only one built-in backend there is a single result list and nothing to fuse.
answer_text:
`RRFRanker` is **not** a single-list re-ranker.

It is a `GroupedRanker`:

> `ReRanker`: operates on a single result list (`LLMReRanker`, `CrossEncoderReRanker`)
> `GroupedRanker`: operates on multiple result groups (`RRFRanker` for fusion)

Docs:

* https://docs.mistral.ai/studio/search/search-toolkit/retrieval/rerankers
* https://docs.mistral.ai/studio/search/search-toolkit/retrieval/retrievers

### When is it right for hybrid search?

Reciprocal Rank Fusion fuses by **rank position**, not raw score:

> `Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) combines results from multiple retrievers using rank positions. Useful for fusing different retrieval strategies on the same index.`

When to use:

> * Combining multiple retrieval strategies on the same index (dense vectors, hybrid search, etc.)
> * Results from multiple sources with incomparable scores
> * No additional model or cost constraints
> * Fusion that doesn't require score normalization

E.g. `dense` query-profile + `hybrid` query-profile, or `VectorRetriever` + `KeywordRetriever`.

### What does it need in front of it?

A `QueryEngine` with a **list of retrievers**:

```python
from mistralai.search.toolkit.retrieval import QueryEngine
from mistralai.search.toolkit.retrieval.retrievers import VectorRetriever, KeywordRetriever
from mistralai.search.toolkit.retrieval.rerankers import RRFRanker

query_engine = QueryEngine(
    retriever=[
        VectorRetriever(client=vector_store, embedder=embedder),
        KeywordRetriever(client=keyword_store),
    ],
    rerankers=[RRFRanker(rrf_k=60, top_k=10)],
)
```

Or two `VectorRetriever`s with different Vespa `query_profile`s:

```python
dense_store = app.get_search_index(config, collection_name="my_collection", query_profile="dense")
hybrid_store = app.get_search_index(config, collection_name="my_collection", query_profile="hybrid")

dense_retriever = VectorRetriever(client=dense_store, embedder=embedder)
hybrid_retriever = VectorRetriever(client=hybrid_store, embedder=embedder)

query_engine = QueryEngine(
    retriever=[dense_retriever, hybrid_retriever],
    rerankers=[RRFRanker(rrf_k=60, top_k=10)],
)
```

Do **not** use `RRFRanker` after a single retriever — use `LLMReRanker` / `CrossEncoderReRanker` for that single-list case.

question: I want to build a Vibe Work assistant that collects expense details via a typed form with a regex-validated receipt ID field, but when validation of the submitted expense fails, the conversation should show a failure. How do I implement the form input, and how do I signal the failure in the output so the workflow is marked as failed?
reference_answer: Define a FormInput subclass with typed fields (e.g., TextField with a pattern like ^RCP-\d{6}$ for the receipt ID) and collect it via wait_for_input. Your workflow must return a ChatAssistantWorkflowOutput to surface in Vibe Work; on validation failure, return it with isError=True and the failure message as text content.
answer_text:
For Vibe Work, build an `InteractiveWorkflow` that returns `ChatAssistantWorkflowOutput`:

### 1. Typed form + regex-validated receipt ID

Use `FormInput` with `TextField(..., pattern=...)`. `pattern` is optional regex validation:

> Docs: [Forms and confirmations](https://docs.mistral.ai/studio/workflows/interacting-with-workflows/conversational_workflows/forms_and_confirmations)

```python
from mistralai.workflows.conversational import FormInput, TextField
import mistralai.workflows as workflows
import mistralai.workflows.plugins.mistralai as workflows_mistralai

class ExpenseForm(FormInput):
    """Structured form for expense submission."""
    description: str = TextField(description="Expense description")
    receipt_id: str = TextField(
        description="Receipt ID",
        pattern=r"^RCP-\d{6}$",
    )

class ExpenseSubmissionWorkflow(workflows.InteractiveWorkflow):
    @workflows.workflow.entrypoint
    async def run(self) -> workflows_mistralai.ChatAssistantWorkflowOutput:
        expense = await self.wait_for_input(
            ExpenseForm,
            label="Submit Expense",
        )
```

This is the documented expense-form example — same field definition for `receipt_id`. Full form also supports `NumberField(minimum, maximum)`, `DateField`, `DateTimeField`, `SingleChoice`, `MultiChoice`, `FileField`.

### 2. Signal validation failure

Return `ChatAssistantWorkflowOutput(..., isError=True)`. The text content becomes the error message, and the workflow is marked as failed in the conversation:

> Docs: [Publish in Vibe - Error handling](https://docs.mistral.ai/studio/workflows/interacting-with-workflows/conversational_workflows/publish_in_vibe)

```python
@workflows.workflow.define(
    name="expense-validation-workflow",
    workflow_display_name="Expense Validation",
    workflow_description="Validates expense data",
)
class ExpenseValidationWorkflow:
    @workflows.workflow.entrypoint
    async def run(self, expense_id: str) -> workflows_mistralai.ChatAssistantWorkflowOutput:
        expense = lookup_expense(expense_id)
        if expense is None:
            return workflows_mistralai.ChatAssistantWorkflowOutput(
                content=[workflows_mistralai.TextOutput(text=f"Expense {expense_id} not found.")],
                isError=True,
            )
        return workflows_mistralai.ChatAssistantWorkflowOutput(
            content=[workflows_mistralai.TextOutput(text=f"Expense {expense_id} is valid.")]
        )
```

Consumer behavior — `Workflow failed: {workflow-name}` display — is described in [Run Workflows in Vibe Work](https://docs.mistral.ai/vibe/work/workflows).

question: Is there a timeout limit for code interpreter executions, and what happens if the executed code exceeds it?
reference_answer: The documentation does not mention any execution timeout limit for the code interpreter or the behavior when a timeout is exceeded.
answer_text:
Based on Mistral's public documentation, **no execution timeout limit for Code Interpreter is documented.**

* The [Code Interpreter](https://docs.mistral.ai/studio/agents/agent-tools/code_interpreter) page describes it only as:

> "safely execute code in an isolated container"

  It covers creation via `tools=[{"type": "code_interpreter"}]` with the Agents API / Conversations API (`/v1/conversations`), and the `tool.execution` output fields `code` / `code_output`, `created_at` / `completed_at` — but states **no duration limit, timeout value, or timeout behavior**.

* The [Tools overview](https://docs.mistral.ai/studio/agents/agent-tools) page likewise states only that built-in tools execute "in our internal environment" — no timeout.

* The [Known limitations](https://docs.mistral.ai/resources/known-limitations) page documents limits for context window, rate limits (`429`), file uploads (`512 MB`), batch, streaming (`10 min inactivity`), function calling (`128 tools`), JSON mode, vision — **no Code Interpreter execution timeout**.

The only sandbox/session timeouts documented are for a different product, [Vibe Code Web Limits and lifecycle](https://docs.mistral.ai/vibe/code/vibe-code-web/limits-and-lifecycle):

* `Maximum session duration: 24 hours`
* `Inactivity timeout while waiting for your reply: 3 hours`

Those do **not** apply to a single Code Interpreter `tool.execution`.

Therefore: there is no publicly documented Code Interpreter per-execution timeout, and no documented "what happens on exceed" behavior such as `TIMED_OUT` / `FAILED` / truncation.

question: In Mistral's Work chat, if I want to fetch live data from a connected tool like Gmail, Drive, or Notion, which feature should I use, and how does it differ from using Web Search?
reference_answer: Use Connectors — they pull live data from tools connected to your account (Gmail, Drive, Notion, etc.). Web Search is instead for getting quick, up-to-date public answers with sources.
answer_text:
In Mistral **Work** chat, use **Connectors** to pull live data from `Gmail`, `Notion`, etc.:

> “Connectors are secure bridges between Work and your external tools and data sources. They let Work retrieve, analyze, and act on data from services like Gmail, Google Drive, GitHub, or Notion as part of a task.”

Docs used:

* [Connect tools with Connectors](https://docs.mistral.ai/vibe/work/connectors)
* [Search the web / Choosing the right tool](https://docs.mistral.ai/vibe/work/web-search-open-url)

**How to use:**

1. `Connectors` page from sidebar > find card e.g. `Gmail` / `Notion` > `Connect` > complete OAuth 2.0 flow.
2. In chat: `+` icon or type `/` > `Tools` > enable the Connector you want.
3. Ask naturally, e.g. “Check my Gmail for unread messages about the quarterly report and summarize them”. Work decides which Connector to call, asks for authentication if missing.

**vs. Web Search:**

Per [Choosing the right tool](https://docs.mistral.ai/vibe/work/web-search-open-url):

* `Pull live data from a connected tool (Gmail, Drive, Notion...)` -> **Connectors**
* `Get a quick, up-to-date answer with sources` / `Analyze a specific page` -> **Web search / Open URL**

Differences:

* **Source:** Connectors = your private authenticated data via OAuth, can also act – e.g. draft/send email, create pages/events, with approval prompt before sensitive actions. Web Search = public internet, browses in real time past model knowledge-cutoff, returns globe icon + inline links to sources.
* **Storage:** `Featured Connectors fetch data in real time for your current request. We don't store it on our servers, and disconnecting revokes access immediately.` – [Connectors](https://docs.mistral.ai/vibe/work/connectors)
* Exception: `Google Drive and Microsoft SharePoint` as **Knowledge Connectors** are indexed/stored for instant search with regular sync, not real-time fetch.

question: I started a coding session in the terminal and want to continue the same work on a repo I haven't cloned locally, in the cloud. What command do I use from the terminal to hand off my work, and what do I give up by not using the editor surface?

answer_text:
From the terminal, hand off with **Teleport to Vibe Code Web**:

> Inside an active local session, run:
> ```
> /teleport
> ```
> The session continues in Vibe Code Web, powered by Mistral Medium 3.5.

That is the one-way `CLI -> cloud` path for `same work, repo you have not cloned, no terminal open`:

* agent clones repo into sandbox, works, streams progress, pushes branch + opens draft PR.
* you follow from any device signed in to Vibe at returned Vibe Code Web URL.

Prerequisites: Pro / Team / Enterprise API key, Mistral GitHub App installed on repo, local session on Mistral model e.g. Medium 3.5 / Devstral, run from inside Git repo.

Docs used:

* [Teleport from CLI to web](https://docs.mistral.ai/vibe/code/cli/teleport-cli-web)
* [Choose CLI, VS Code, or web sessions](https://docs.mistral.ai/vibe/code/choose-cli-vscode-web-sessions)

### What you give up vs editor surface

Editor surface = **VS Code extension**:

> **CLI and VS Code extension share the same configuration and sessions** (agents, skills, MCP servers, profiles, and conversation history). You can start a session in the CLI and resume it in the extension, or the other way around, without losing context.

|---|---|---|
| Install | Required local | None |

| FS / shell | Local working tree, through ACP | Remote sandbox |
| Non-interactive | No – same as Web | No – only CLI has `vibe --prompt` |

1. **Bidirectional continuity:** `Teleport is one-way. Once a session moves to the cloud, you can't pull it back into the local CLI. Continue from Vibe Code Web.`
2. **Local working-tree access:** no local files / services / secrets.
3. **Model choice:** `Cloud sessions run on Mistral Medium 3.5, regardless of local model.`

question: What is the maximum retention period for a SCIM sync run's result before it is deleted, and can completed runs be purged early via the API?
reference_answer: The documentation does not specify any retention period for sync run records or any endpoint to delete or purge completed runs.
answer_text:
Based on Mistral's published documentation, **no maximum retention / deletion period and no early-purge API for SCIM sync runs is documented.**

The only documented SCIM sync-run API surface is:

* `POST /v1/admin/scim/sync` - Trigger an on-demand SCIM synchronization for the Organization.
  > "Requires SAML authentication to be enabled and the Organization to be in SCIM user provisioning mode. A dry run previews every change without applying it; a real run applies the categories selected in `sync_config`. Only one run may be active at a time — a conflicting request returns the already-active run."
  * https://docs.mistral.ai/api/endpoint/beta/admin/scim

* `GET /v1/admin/scim/sync/{run_id}` - Retrieve an on-demand SCIM synchronization run for the Organization.
  > "Returns the run's lifecycle status along with the preview or result summary once the synchronization plan has been built."
  > Fields: `created_at`, `dry_run`, `error_message`, `finished_at`, `run_id`, `started_at`, `status: "PENDING"|"RUNNING"|"SUCCESS"|"SKIPPED"|"FAILED"`, `summary: ScimSyncSummaryOut | null`, `sync_config`
  * https://docs.mistral.ai/api/endpoint/beta/admin/scim

That reference lists **no**:

1. `DELETE /v1/admin/scim/sync/{run_id}` or other purge/cleanup operation,
2. `finished_at + X days -> deleted` retention statement,
3. result-summary expiry.

Therefore:

* **Maximum retention before deletion: not stated in docs.**
* **Can completed runs be purged early via API: No — no purge/delete endpoint is exposed in the Beta Admin Scim API reference.**

If you need a guaranteed retention/purge SLA, contact Mistral support / your Enterprise admin, as SCIM requires Enterprise SAML + SCIM provisioning mode.

reference_answer: Conversation deletions are recorded in audit logs (e.g., le Chat conversation deletion events), which are available by default on Enterprise plans. question: What are some common use cases for fine-tuning a model instead of relying on prompting?
reference_answer: Common use cases include customizing response format and tone, specializing the model for a specific domain, distilling behavior from a stronger model, mimicking a complex prompt without needing it (saving tokens and reducing costs), and reducing cost and latency with a small but efficient fine-tuned model.
answer_text:
Per Mistral docs, start with prompt engineering as it's faster and less resource-intensive, then consider fine-tuning when you need better alignment, efficiency, or new knowledge:

Common use cases for fine-tuning instead of prompting ([Fine-tuning](https://docs.mistral.ai/resources/deprecated/finetuning)):

* **Customizing format and tone:** generate responses in a specific format and tone
* **Domain specialization:** specialize for a specific topic/domain to improve performance on domain-specific tasks. Current guide describes this as customizing and optimizing performance for specific use cases by training on a labeled dataset ([Fine-tuning Guide](https://docs.mistral.ai/guides/finetuning)).
* **Distillation from stronger model:** train a smaller model to mimic behavior of larger model
* **Compress complex prompts:** mimic behavior of a model with a complex prompt without the actual prompt, saving tokens and cost
* **Reduce cost/latency:** use a small yet efficient fine-tuned model that works better than a larger generic model, faster/cheaper because it doesn't require very long prompt
* **Teach new facts/workflows:** e.g. advanced tools or complicated workflows

Benefits vs prompting per same page: works significantly better than prompting, better alignment because specifically trained on these tasks.

question: What file formats and what maximum size can I upload for OCR? A .zip upload comes back as 422 `Invalid file format.`
reference_answer:
OCR accepts PDF, Office documents (DOCX, PPTX, XLSX/CSV), text formats such as TXT, EPUB, RTF, ODT and LaTeX, and images (JPEG, PNG, AVIF, TIFF, GIF, HEIC, BMP, WebP); ZIP is not among them.
Uploads are capped at 512 MB, OCR documents at 50 MB and 1,000 pages, and files are kept 30 days.

question: Can I use `KeywordRetriever` against the Vespa backend? Passing a keyword query to it raises a pydantic ValidationError.
reference_answer:
No: the built-in Vespa and Postgres backends do not implement `KeywordStoreIndex`, so `KeywordRetriever` needs a custom keyword store.
For hybrid search on a built-in backend use `VectorRetriever`, which sends the query text and the embedding together.
answer_text:
No — you cannot use `KeywordRetriever` against the Vespa backend.

The built-in Vespa backend does not implement `KeywordStoreIndex`, so `KeywordRetriever` requires a custom keyword store instead [1]. For hybrid search with a built-in backend, use `VectorRetriever`; it sends both the query text and embedding to the backend [1].

That mismatch is why passing a keyword query to `KeywordRetriever` backed by Vespa raises a pydantic `ValidationError` — Vespa is not a valid `KeywordStoreIndex` client.

question: A one-page 308 kB PDF sent as base64 to Document QnA reports 321,774 prompt tokens and 400s — what is the context limit and why is the document so expensive?
reference_answer:
Document QnA has its own document and page limits, and the request still has to fit the model's context window — 256k tokens on Medium 3.5, Small 4 and Large 3, 128k on Medium 3.1.
Requests over the window come back as 400, and token counts cover input plus output.
answer_text:
Your **321,774 prompt tokens exceed context**:

* `mistral-small-latest` is `mistral-small-2603` / Mistral Small 4 [1](https://docs.mistral.ai/models/mistral-small-4-0-26-03#:~:text=%7C%20API%20names%20%7C%20mistral%2Dsmall%2D2603%2C%20mistral%2Dsmall%2Dlatest%20%7C), whose max is `256k tokens` [1](https://docs.mistral.ai/resources/known-limitations#context-window:~:text=%7C%20Mistral%20Small%204%20%7C%20256k%20tokens%20%7C).
  * `321,774 > 256,000`, so the request is over-limit — expected failure mode is error / extreme `400s` processing.

* This is **not** a file limit violation: `Uploaded document files must not exceed 50 MB in size and should be no longer than 1,000 pages.` [2](https://docs.mistral.ai/studio/document-processing/document_qna#are-there-any-limits-regarding-the-document-qna-api:~:text=Uploaded%20document%20files%20must%20not%20exceed%2050%20MB%20in%20size%20and%20should%20be%20no%20longer%20than%201%2C000%20pages.) — your `308 kB, 1-page` PDF passes that.

Why so expensive:

* `You can perform QnA with any PDF by encoding them in base64 and sending them as part of the chat completion request.` [3](https://docs.mistral.ai/studio/document-processing/document_qna#usage:~:text=You%20can%20perform%20QnA%20with%20any%20PDF%20by%20encoding%20them%20in%20base64%20and%20sending%20them%20as%20part%20of%20the%20chat%20completion%20request.)
* i.e. base64 inflates size ~33% and the whole document is billed as `prompt_tokens` on every call. A dense / image-heavy 308 kB PDF can therefore expand to hundreds of thousands of tokens.

Fix: don't resend base64 per question — upload once and reference `file_id` / `document_url`, reduce pages/resolution, or use OCR + text extraction first.

[1] https://docs.mistral.ai/resources/known-limitations#context-window:~:text=%7C%20Mistral%20Small%204%20%7C%20256k%20tokens%20%7C

question: Which models can take a document as input in a chat message, and how do I pass it?
reference_answer:
Document QnA is the documented path: send a `document_url` content chunk alongside your `text` chunk, with a publicly reachable URL or a base64 data URI.
The worked examples run it on `mistral-small-latest`.
answer_text:
34 models support Document QnA (`document-qna`), including Mistral Small / Medium / Large, Ministral, Pixtral, Codestral, Devstral, Magistral, Voxtral and others [1].

> “[Document QnA](https://docs.mistral.ai/studio/document-processing/document_qna) (`document-qna`), 34 models: Codestral (`codestral-2501`), Codestral (`codestral-2508`), Devstral 2 (`devstral-2512`)...” [1]

See full list on [Model capability matrix](https://docs.mistral.ai/models).

How to pass it:

Send a `user` message with `content` as list containing `text` + `document_url`:

```json
{
  "model": "mistral-small-latest",
  "messages": [{
    "role": "user",
    "content": [
      {"type": "text", "text": "what is the last sentence in the document"},
      {"type": "document_url", "document_url": "https://arxiv.org/pdf/1805.04770"}
    ]
  }]
}
```

Options for `document_url`:

- Public PDF URL — “Be sure the URL is **public** and accessible by our API.” [2]
- Base64: “You can perform QnA with any PDF by encoding them in base64 and sending them as part of the chat completion request.” [3] — use `data:application/pdf;base64,<base64_pdf>`
- Uploaded file signed URL: upload with `purpose="ocr"`, get signed URL, then “You can now query any LLM with the signed url.” [4]

Limits: “Uploaded document files must not exceed 50 MB in size and should be no longer than 1,000 pages.” [5]

question: How do I count the tokens of a prompt locally, before sending the request?
reference_answer:
The documentation does not describe a local tokenizer or a token-counting endpoint.
It reports token usage only in the response of a call that has already been made.
answer_text:
Count tokens locally with the official Mistral tokenizer [1]:

```bash
pip install mistral-common
```

```python
from mistral_common.tokens.tokenizers.mistral import MistralTokenizer

tokenizer = MistralTokenizer.v3()
result = tokenizer.encode_chat_completion(
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Hello, world!"}]
)
print(result.tokens)
print(len(result.tokens))  # token count
```

> The docs state: “Install the official Mistral tokenizer” with `pip install mistral-common` and “Use it to tokenize text” via `MistralTokenizer.v3()` + `encode_chat_completion()` [1].

Use `encode_chat_completion()` — not raw string tokenization — so chat formatting / special tokens are counted correctly.

Sources:
[1] https://docs.mistral.ai/resources/migration-guides#migrate-from-llama

* `reasoning_effort = "none"`: The model thinks minimally and the thinking chunk is omitted from the response. [1]

- `conversation.response.done`: The response is done and finished [1].
- `conversation.response.error`: An error occurred [1].
- `message.output.delta`: Chunk of content, usually tokens corresponding to the model reply [1].

- `tool.execution.done`: A tool has finished executing [1].
- `agent.handoff.started`: The handoff to a different agent has started [1].
- `agent.handoff.done`: The handoff was concluded [1].
- `function.call.delta`: Chunk of content, usually tokens corresponding to the function tool call [1].

question: What do `tool_choice` and `parallel_tool_calls` do on a chat completion request, and which values does `tool_choice` take?
reference_answer:
`tool_choice` is `none` (never call a tool), `auto` (model decides), `any`/`required` (must call one or more), or `{"type": "function", "function": {"name": ...}}` to force one tool.
`parallel_tool_calls` enables the model to call several tools in one turn.
answer_text:
`tool_choice` controls which (if any) tool the model calls [1]:

> “Controls which (if any) tool is called by the model. `none` means the model will not call any tool and instead generates a message. `auto` means the model can pick between generating a message or calling one or more tools. `any` or `required` means the model must call one or more tools. Specifying a particular tool via `{"type": "function", "function": {"name": "my_function"}}` forces the model to call that tool.”[1]

The Function Calling guide summarizes the same modes as:

> “Developers can use `tool_choice` to specify how tools are used: - "auto": default mode. Model decides if it uses the tool or not. - "any": forces tool use. - "none": prevents tool use.”[3]

Values: `auto`, `any` / `required`, `none`, or a specific function object `{"type": "function", "function": {"name": "my_function"}}` [1].

`parallel_tool_calls` (boolean, optional):

> “Whether to enable parallel function calling during tool use, when enabled the model can call multiple tools in parallel.”[2]

question: What must a migration define before `mistral-vespa migrate` will deploy it?
reference_answer:
A migration subclasses `VespaMigration` and its `migrate()` must set the application name and create at least one schema.
The deploy step then builds the application package from the whole migration chain.
answer_text:
Before `mistral-vespa migrate` will deploy it, a migration must be a `VespaMigration` subclass implementing `migrate()` [1]. The first migration must call `set_app_name(name)` [2], with a lowercase-letters-only name [3]. Schema definition must use `create_schema` with an explicit `indexing_mode` [4], with `DOCUMENT_PER_CHUNK` recommended [5]. `migrate` then discovers migrations, runs them in order, builds the app package, and uploads it [6].

question: Which models take `reasoning_effort`, and what does each value do?
reference_answer:
`mistral-small-latest` and `mistral-medium-3-5` accept `reasoning_effort` on any chat completion, with `high` recommended for agentic and code work.
`high` returns a full thinking chunk before the answer; `none` makes the model think minimally and omits the chunk.

question: Deploying my migration fails with `String should match pattern '^[a-z]+$'` on the application name — what characters may an application name contain?
reference_answer:
The name passed to `set_app_name()` may contain only lowercase letters a-z; digits, underscores, hyphens and other characters are rejected.
The collection name passed to `create_schema()` is a separate value and is not bound by that rule.

question: Where do I see the per-model rate limits configured for my organization?
